options: 401, because the fallback policy applies to requests that match no endpoint
200 with the file, because the static file middleware answers before authorization runs
302 to the login path, because static files inherit the default cookie challenge
404, because files in `wwwroot` must be mapped as endpoints to be served
questions.explanation: Static File Middleware short-circuits the pipeline when it finds a matching file, so with `UseStaticFiles` ahead of `UseAuthorization` the fallback policy never sees the request and the file is public (verified: 200). The fallback policy would apply only if the request reached the authorization middleware without an endpoint. There is no cookie scheme here to redirect, and `UseStaticFiles` serves `wwwroot` without any endpoint mapping.

questions.prompt: With a `FallbackPolicy` that requires an authenticated user, moving `app.UseStaticFiles()` to after `app.UseAuthorization()` makes an anonymous request for an existing `wwwroot` file get a 401.
questions.explanation: A request for a file matches no endpoint, and the authorization middleware applies the fallback policy to such requests, so it challenges before Static File Middleware runs (verified: 401 after the move, 200 before it). This is the documented way to protect static files: place `UseStaticFiles` after `UseAuthorization` and rely on the fallback policy, or serve protected files from an action that returns `File(...)`.

questions.prompt: `wwwroot/data.blob` exists, `.blob` is not in the default content type mappings, and the app calls `app.UseStaticFiles()` with no options. What does `GET /data.blob` return?
options: 200 with `Content-Type: application/octet-stream`
200 with no `Content-Type` header
404 Not Found
415 Unsupported Media Type
questions.explanation: Static File Middleware serves only files whose extension the `FileExtensionContentTypeProvider` knows; an unknown extension is treated as not found, so the request falls through and ends in 404 (verified). Setting `ServeUnknownFileTypes = true` serves it (with `DefaultContentType` if you set one), and adding the extension to the provider's `Mappings` is the safer fix. 415 is about request bodies, not file downloads.

options: 200 with `index.html`, because the two middlewares can run in either order
301 redirect to `/index.html`
200 with a directory listing of `wwwroot`
404, because `UseDefaultFiles` only rewrites the path and nothing after it serves the file
questions.explanation: `UseDefaultFiles` is a URL rewriter: it changes `/` to `/index.html` but does not send the file. It must run before `UseStaticFiles`; in the order shown, the static file middleware has already passed on `/`, so the request ends in 404 (verified). It does not redirect to `/index.html`, and directory listings need `UseDirectoryBrowser`.

questions.prompt: Which statements about serving files with ASP.NET Core's static file middleware are true?
options: `app.UseFileServer()` combines static files and default documents, but leaves directory browsing off
With `UseDefaultFiles`, a request for `/docs` (no trailing slash) to a folder with `index.html` is redirected to `/docs/`
`UseStaticFiles(new StaticFileOptions { FileProvider = new PhysicalFileProvider(dir), RequestPath = "/files" })` serves `dir/a.txt` at `/files/a.txt`
`app.UseStaticFiles()` serves files from the content root when `wwwroot` does not contain them
Directory browsing is on by default in Development
questions.explanation: `UseFileServer()` is `UseDefaultFiles` plus `UseStaticFiles`; directory browsing needs `enableDirectoryBrowsing: true` (verified: 404 without it, a listing with it). Default documents for a folder requested without the trailing slash produce a 301 to the slashed URL (verified). A `PhysicalFileProvider` with a `RequestPath` maps another folder under a URL prefix. Plain `UseStaticFiles()` uses only the web root, and directory browsing is off in every environment because it can expose files.

questions.prompt: A browser fetches `/app.js` twice from an app using `app.UseStaticFiles()`, and the file does not change in between. Put these steps in order, first to last.
options: The middleware returns 200 with the file plus `ETag` and `Last-Modified` headers
The browser stores the response along with its validators
The browser sends the second request with `If-None-Match` set to the stored ETag
The middleware compares that value with the current file's ETag
The middleware returns 304 Not Modified without a body
questions.explanation: Static File Middleware adds `ETag` and `Last-Modified` to every file response. A later conditional request carries `If-None-Match` (or `If-Modified-Since`); when the validator still matches, the middleware answers 304 with no body (verified with curl), and the browser reuses its copy. The 304 cannot come before the browser has a validator to send.

questions.prompt: A .NET 9 app replaces `app.UseStaticFiles()` with `app.MapStaticAssets()`. A background job later writes a new file `wwwroot/reports/today.pdf` while the app runs. What happens to requests for it?
options: `MapStaticAssets` serves it, compressed on the fly with Brotli
It is not served by `MapStaticAssets`, which serves assets from a manifest built at build or publish time
It is served, but without an `ETag`, because strong ETags come from the build manifest
The app restarts to rebuild the asset manifest, then serves the file
questions.explanation: `MapStaticAssets` (new in .NET 9) uses a manifest produced at build/publish time to serve known assets with precompressed gzip/Brotli variants, content-based ETags and fingerprinted URLs. Files that appear at runtime are not in that manifest, so they need `UseStaticFiles` or another endpoint. It does not compress unknown files on the fly or restart the app.

questions.prompt: An app calls `app.UseStaticFiles()` with default options. Which statements about its responses are true?
options: Responses include an `ETag` header
Responses include a `Last-Modified` header
Responses include `Cache-Control: max-age=604800` unless you change it
`OnPrepareResponse` can add a `Cache-Control` header to each file response
The file is served compressed when the client sends `Accept-Encoding: br`
questions.explanation: The middleware sets `ETag` and `Last-Modified` (so conditional requests can get 304) but no `Cache-Control` at all by default (verified). To add caching headers you set them in `StaticFileOptions.OnPrepareResponse`. `UseStaticFiles` does not compress; precompressed assets come from `MapStaticAssets` in .NET 9, or you add response compression yourself.

questions.prompt: With `app.MapFallbackToFile("index.html")` in a single-page app, a `GET /assets/missing.js` for a file that does not exist returns `index.html` with status 200.
questions.explanation: `MapFallbackToFile` uses the route pattern `{*path:nonfile}`, and the `nonfile` constraint excludes paths that look like file names (with an extension). A missing `.js` therefore gets 404 (verified), which avoids sending HTML to a script tag, while client-side routes such as `/orders/42` get `index.html` with 200.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: building an HS256 JWT by hand and checking the signature after changing the payload.
questions.explanation: A JWT is three base64url segments joined by dots; the header `{"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}` always encodes to `eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9`. The payload is only encoded, so anyone can decode it and read the claims. The signature is an HMAC over `header.payload`, so swapping in a payload with `role: admin` gives a different HMAC and the check prints `False`, while the original segments still verify.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: base64 versus base64url for the same bytes, and decoding the base64url form with `Convert.FromBase64String`.
questions.explanation: Base64url (RFC 4648) replaces `+` with `-` and `/` with `_`, and JWTs also drop the `=` padding. `Convert.FromBase64String` accepts only standard base64, so the URL-safe string throws `FormatException`. After switching the characters back and padding the length to a multiple of four, it decodes to the original 4 bytes.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: reading `exp` from a JWT payload and applying a 5-minute clock skew.
questions.explanation: `exp` is a NumericDate: seconds since the Unix epoch, so `FromUnixTimeSeconds` gives 2025-10-09, while reading it as milliseconds lands in January 1970. With a 5-minute skew a token is still accepted until `exp + 300s`: 120 and 300 seconds late pass, 301 seconds late is rejected. This mirrors the JWT handler, whose `ClockSkew` defaults to 5 minutes.

questions.prompt: An API uses `AddJwtBearer` and does not set `ClockSkew`. A client sends a correctly signed token whose `exp` was 3 minutes ago. What does an `[Authorize]` endpoint return?
options: 200, because the default clock skew of 5 minutes still accepts the token
401, because lifetime validation compares `exp` with the current time exactly
200, because `ValidateLifetime` is off unless you turn it on
401 for the first request, then 200 after the handler refreshes the token
questions.explanation: `TokenValidationParameters.ClockSkew` defaults to 300 seconds, so a token expired less than 5 minutes ago still validates (verified: 200 at 3 minutes, 401 at 6 minutes). Set `ClockSkew = TimeSpan.Zero` when short-lived tokens must expire on time. `ValidateLifetime` is on by default, and the bearer handler never refreshes tokens; that is the client's job.

questions.prompt: A client calls a JWT-protected endpoint with a correctly signed token that expired an hour ago. Which header does the 401 response carry in .NET 8?
options: `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer`
`WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token", error_description="The token expired at '...'"`
`WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="expired_token"`
`WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_scope", error_description="Token lifetime exceeded"`
questions.explanation: When a token was sent but failed validation, the bearer handler adds the RFC 6750 `invalid_token` error and, by default (`IncludeErrorDetails = true`), a description; for an expired token it is "The token expired at '<time>'" (verified). A plain `Bearer` with no error is what a request without any token gets. `expired_token` is not an RFC 6750 code, and `insufficient_scope` is for a valid token that lacks rights.

questions.prompt: When a valid JWT reaches an endpoint whose role policy the user fails, the JWT bearer handler answers 403 with a `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_scope"` header.
questions.explanation: The handler's forbid action just sets 403; it adds no `WWW-Authenticate` header (verified with curl). `WWW-Authenticate` comes from the challenge, which produces a 401 for missing or invalid tokens. RFC 6750 defines `insufficient_scope`, but ASP.NET Core does not emit it unless you write that yourself in `OnForbidden`.

questions.prompt: A token contains `"sub": "u1"`, `"role": "admin"` and `"name": "ann"`. The API uses `AddJwtBearer` with default claim mapping. What do `User.FindFirstValue(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier)`, `User.IsInRole("admin")` and `User.Identity.Name` return?
options: `null`, `true`, `"ann"`
`"u1"`, `true`, `null`
`null`, `false`, `null`
questions.explanation: With `MapInboundClaims` on (the default), `sub` becomes `ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier` and `role` becomes `ClaimTypes.Role`, so the first two calls give `"u1"` and `true`. The `name` claim is not mapped (the legacy mapping turns `unique_name` into `ClaimTypes.Name`), so `Identity.Name`, which reads `ClaimTypes.Name`, is `null` (verified). Set `TokenValidationParameters.NameClaimType = "name"` to fix it.

questions.prompt: An API sets `options.MapInboundClaims = false` in `AddJwtBearer` and changes nothing else. A token has `sub`, `role` and `name` claims. Which statements are true?
options: The claim types on `User` are the short names `sub`, `role` and `name`
`User.FindFirstValue(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier)` returns `null`
`User.IsInRole("admin")` returns `false` until `RoleClaimType` is set to `"role"`
`User.Identity.Name` returns the `name` claim, because the name claim type switches to `name` automatically
Tokens are rejected, because `sub` no longer matches the expected claim type
questions.explanation: Turning mapping off keeps the JWT's own claim names (verified: `sub=u1;role=admin;name=ann`), so lookups by the long `ClaimTypes` URIs find nothing. `IsInRole` and `Identity.Name` use `RoleClaimType` and `NameClaimType`, which still default to the long URIs, so you set them to `"role"` and `"name"` yourself. Validation itself does not depend on claim names, so tokens are still accepted.

questions.prompt: Browsers can't set an `Authorization` header on WebSocket connections, so a SignalR client sends its JWT as `?access_token=...`. How does the server accept it?
options: Set `options.SaveToken = true`, which also reads the token from the query string
Add `[FromQuery] string access_token` to the hub's `OnConnectedAsync` and validate it there
In `JwtBearerEvents.OnMessageReceived`, copy the query value into `context.Token` for hub paths
Set `TokenValidationParameters.TokenReader` to a delegate that returns the query value
questions.explanation: The bearer handler reads only the `Authorization` header by default; `OnMessageReceived` runs first and can set `context.Token`, and the docs restrict this to the hub path so tokens in URLs aren't accepted everywhere (verified: the hub path returned 200, another path 401). `SaveToken` only stores the validated token in the authentication properties. Validating inside the hub is too late for `[Authorize]`, and `TokenReader` parses a token string, it does not locate it.

questions.prompt: Which statements about JWT signing keys and `AddJwtBearer` are true?
options: With `Authority` set, the handler downloads the OpenID Connect metadata and the signing keys from its `jwks_uri`
With HS256, every API that validates tokens needs the same secret the issuer signs with
With RS256, an API needs just the issuer's public key to validate tokens
RS256 encrypts the payload, so clients can't read the claims
Publishing an HS256 key in a JWKS document is safe, because the document is read-only
questions.explanation: Setting `Authority` makes the handler fetch `/.well-known/openid-configuration` and the keys listed at `jwks_uri`, refreshing them for key rotation. HS256 is symmetric, so anyone who can validate can also mint tokens; RS256 signs with a private key and validates with the public key. Signing doesn't hide the payload (that needs JWE), and publishing a symmetric key lets anyone forge tokens.

questions.prompt: An API that validates self-contained JWTs can invalidate one specific token before its `exp` without keeping any server-side state, such as a deny list or a token version per user.
questions.explanation: A self-contained JWT is accepted by signature and claims alone, so the server has nothing to change for a single token. Revocation needs state the API checks, such as a deny list of `jti` values, a per-user token version or security stamp, or very short access tokens combined with revocable refresh tokens. Rotating the signing key invalidates every token, not one.

questions.prompt: What does running `dotnet user-jwts create` in an ASP.NET Core project with JWT bearer authentication do?
options: It creates a development token, stores the signing key in user secrets and adds issuer and audience settings to `appsettings.Development.json`
It registers the app with Microsoft Entra ID and downloads a token signed by Entra for local testing
It generates an RSA key pair, writes the private key into `appsettings.json` and prints a token signed with it
It starts a local token server on port 5001 that issues tokens to the app until the tool stops
questions.explanation: `dotnet user-jwts` is a development tool that mints a token locally, keeps the signing key in the project's user secrets and writes `Authentication:Schemes:Bearer` settings (valid audiences and issuer) into `appsettings.Development.json`, so `AddJwtBearer` accepts the token without an identity provider. It does not talk to Entra ID, run a server or put keys in `appsettings.json`.

questions.prompt: A SPA's 10-minute access token has expired, and it holds a refresh token. Put these steps in order, first to last.
options: The SPA calls the API with the expired access token
The API answers 401 with `error="invalid_token"`
The SPA sends the refresh token to the token endpoint
The token server checks the refresh token, rotates it and issues a new access token
The SPA retries the original API call with the new access token
questions.explanation: The API validates only the access token, so the expired token earns a 401 with `invalid_token`. The client then uses its refresh token at the token endpoint (never at the API); the server checks it against its store, and with rotation replaces it with a new one. Only then can the client retry the failed call with the fresh access token.

questions.prompt: An app has a `Cookies` scheme for its pages and a `Bearer` scheme for API clients. It registers `AddPolicyScheme("Smart", ...)` with a `ForwardDefaultSelector` that returns `"Bearer"` when the `Authorization` header starts with `Bearer `, otherwise `"Cookies"`, and makes `Smart` the default. What does the policy scheme do?
options: It runs both handlers on each request and merges their claims into one identity
It chooses one of the two schemes per request and forwards authenticate, challenge and forbid to it
It tries `Bearer` first and falls back to `Cookies` when token validation fails
It converts a valid cookie into a bearer token so the API endpoints see one scheme
questions.explanation: A policy scheme has no handler logic of its own: `ForwardDefaultSelector` picks a target scheme for each request, and authenticate, challenge, forbid, sign-in and sign-out are forwarded there. So a browser gets cookie behaviour (redirects) and an API client gets bearer behaviour (401). It doesn't merge identities or retry another scheme after a failure, and nothing turns cookies into tokens.

questions.prompt: A Minimal API endpoint copies `HttpRequest.Body` into a stream. With default Kestrel settings and no size attributes, a client POSTs a 31 MB body. What does the client get?
options: 200, because Kestrel imposes no body size limit by default
400 Bad Request, because the body is larger than the 28 MB `MaxRequestLineSize`
413 Payload Too Large, because the default `MaxRequestBodySize` is 30,000,000 bytes
431 Request Header Fields Too Large, because the `Content-Length` value is over the limit
questions.explanation: Kestrel's `MaxRequestBodySize` defaults to 30,000,000 bytes (about 28.6 MB); reading past it throws `BadHttpRequestException` and the response is 413 (verified with a real 31 MB upload; exactly 30,000,000 bytes succeeded). `MaxRequestLineSize` limits the request line, not the body, and 431 is about header size.

questions.prompt: Kestrel's `MaxRequestBodySize` is set to 1,000 bytes. Which statements are true for Minimal API endpoints that read the body?
options: An endpoint with `[RequestSizeLimit(2000)]` accepts a 1,500-byte body
An endpoint with `[DisableRequestSizeLimit]` accepts a 6,000-byte body
A chunked request with no `Content-Length` is not counted against the limit
Code can raise the limit through `IHttpMaxRequestBodySizeFeature` after it has started reading the body
A 3,000-byte body to an endpoint with no attribute gets 413
questions.explanation: Per-endpoint metadata overrides the server-wide value in both directions (verified: 1,500 bytes accepted with `[RequestSizeLimit(2000)]`, 6,000 with `[DisableRequestSizeLimit]`, 413 without either). The limit also counts bytes as they arrive, so a chunked upload gets 413 too. `IHttpMaxRequestBodySizeFeature.IsReadOnly` becomes true once the body is being read, so the limit must be changed before that.

questions.prompt: A Kestrel endpoint `http://localhost:5000` uses the default protocols (`Http1AndHttp2`). A gRPC client connects with HTTP/2 "prior knowledge" (h2c, no TLS). What happens?
options: Kestrel switches to HTTP/2 after reading the connection preface
The connection fails, because without TLS the endpoint runs HTTP/1.1, so h2c needs `Protocols = Http2`
Kestrel upgrades the connection with an `Upgrade: h2c` response header
Kestrel redirects the client to an HTTPS endpoint with a 307
questions.explanation: Kestrel picks HTTP/2 on an `Http1AndHttp2` endpoint through TLS ALPN; without TLS there's no negotiation, so it speaks HTTP/1.1 and the h2c preface fails (verified: the curl prior-knowledge request failed, and succeeded once `Protocols` was `Http2`). Kestrel does not support the `Upgrade: h2c` mechanism, and it never redirects by itself.

questions.prompt: A .NET 8 app enables `HttpProtocols.Http1AndHttp2AndHttp3` on an HTTPS endpoint. Why does the browser's first request still use HTTP/2?
options: HTTP/3 is reserved for requests after the TLS session is resumed
Kestrel serves HTTP/3 to gRPC clients and HTTP/2 to browsers
HTTP/3 must be confirmed by a DNS SVCB record before Kestrel will accept it
The browser learns about HTTP/3 from the `alt-svc` response header and switches on later requests
questions.explanation: HTTP/3 runs over QUIC on UDP, so a browser first connects over TCP (HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2); Kestrel adds an `alt-svc: h3=":port"` header, and the browser uses HTTP/3 for later requests. Kestrel does not pick the protocol by client type, and it doesn't require DNS records (browsers may use them, but `alt-svc` is what Kestrel provides). Kestrel also needs the QUIC library (msquic) on the host.

questions.prompt: An app runs behind Nginx, which terminates TLS and sets `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto`. Which statements about Forwarded Headers Middleware are true?
options: `new ForwardedHeadersOptions()` has `ForwardedHeaders = None`, so you must choose which headers to process
By default, forwarded headers are accepted from loopback proxies alone (`127.0.0.0/8` and `::1`)
Without the middleware, `UseHttpsRedirection` sees `http` and can redirect every request in a loop
Register `UseForwardedHeaders` after `UseAuthentication` so authentication sees the proxy's address
The middleware is enabled automatically in Production builds
questions.explanation: The options default to `ForwardedHeaders.None`, `ForwardLimit = 1`, `KnownNetworks` 127.0.0.0/8 and `KnownProxies` ::1 (verified by printing them), so a proxy on another address must be added. Without the middleware, `Request.Scheme` stays `http`, and HTTPS redirection keeps redirecting a client that already used HTTPS. The middleware should run before other middleware, and it is added automatically only when `ASPNETCORE_FORWARDEDHEADERS_ENABLED=true`.

questions.prompt: A client calls `https://shop.example.com` through a TLS-terminating proxy at `10.0.0.5`, which is in `KnownProxies`. The app calls `UseForwardedHeaders` then `UseHttpsRedirection`. Put these steps in order, first to last.
options: The proxy decrypts the HTTPS request
The proxy forwards it over HTTP with `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto: https`
Kestrel accepts the connection from `10.0.0.5` with scheme `http`
Forwarded Headers Middleware sets `Request.Scheme` to `https` and `RemoteIpAddress` to the client's address
`UseHttpsRedirection` sees `https` and passes the request on
questions.explanation: The proxy terminates TLS and must add the forwarded headers before Kestrel ever sees the request. Kestrel only knows the proxy's connection, so the scheme is `http` and the remote address is `10.0.0.5`. Because the proxy is trusted, the middleware rewrites the scheme and client IP, and only then does HTTPS redirection run and see a secure request instead of redirecting.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: checking an IPv4-mapped IPv6 remote address against an IPv4 network.
questions.explanation: On a dual-mode socket the remote address can arrive as `::ffff:10.0.5.20`, which is an IPv6 address (`InterNetworkV6`) even though it wraps an IPv4 one. `IPNetwork.Contains` returns false when the families differ, so the check against `10.0.0.0/16` fails until the address is converted with `MapToIPv4()`. This is why the proxy docs tell you to account for mapped addresses when filling `KnownProxies`/`KnownNetworks`.

questions.prompt: A .NET 8 app receives SIGTERM while 20 requests are in flight and does not change any host options. What do Kestrel and the host do?
options: Kestrel stops accepting new connections and waits for in-flight requests until `ShutdownTimeout`, 30 seconds by default
Kestrel aborts the in-flight requests at once and the process exits with code 143
Kestrel keeps accepting connections until in-flight requests reach zero, then stops
The host waits 5 seconds by default, then aborts the remaining requests
questions.explanation: On a stop signal the host stops the server: Kestrel closes its listeners and lets in-flight requests finish, bounded by `HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout`, whose default is 30 seconds since .NET 6 (verified by printing the option). Before .NET 6 the default was 5 seconds. Requests still running when the timeout elapses are aborted; new connections are refused as soon as shutdown starts.

questions.prompt: An ASP.NET Core app runs on IIS with the ASP.NET Core Module set to the in-process hosting model. Which server handles the HTTP requests?
options: Kestrel, inside the app's own `dotnet.exe` process behind IIS
IIS HTTP Server (`IISHttpServer`), inside the IIS worker process `w3wp.exe`
HTTP.sys, which IIS hands requests to after authentication
Kestrel, inside `w3wp.exe`, listening on a loopback port
questions.explanation: In-process hosting loads the app into the IIS worker process and uses IIS HTTP Server instead of Kestrel, which avoids the loopback hop. The out-of-process model is the one where IIS acts as a reverse proxy to Kestrel running in a separate process. HTTP.sys is a separate Windows-only server you choose with `UseHttpSys`, not part of IIS hosting.

questions.prompt: By default, Kestrel enforces a minimum request body data rate of 240 bytes per second with a 5-second grace period, and drops slower uploads.
questions.explanation: `KestrelServerLimits.MinRequestBodyDataRate` defaults to 240 bytes/second with a 5-second grace period (verified by printing the limits), which defends against slow-upload attacks. A request that falls below it times out. You can relax it per request through `IHttpMinRequestBodyDataRateFeature`, for example for slow clients on long uploads.
